zebralogic.title: Preserve exact case of attribute values
zebralogic.principle: Copy every attribute value (names, heights, phones, etc.) exactly as it appears in the problem statement, preserving spelling, punctuation and capitalization. Without this, the verifier will reject the answer due to case mismatches.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: Whenever you output any attribute value in the final grid.
zebralogic.example: Writing "Huawei P50" instead of the required lower‑case "huawei p50".

zebralogic.title: Direct adjacency (directly left of)
zebralogic.principle: Interpret clues that say "X is directly left of Y" as X's house number = Y's house number − 1, preserving left‑right orientation. Without this, you may treat the relation as a loose ordering and lose the required adjacency.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue contains the phrase "directly left of" (or "directly right of").
zebralogic.example: Placing X two houses left of Y when the clue required them to be adjacent.

zebralogic.title: Relative ordering (somewhere left of)
zebralogic.principle: Treat clues that say "X is somewhere to the left of Y" as a strict ordering constraint X < Y, without requiring adjacency. Without this, you might incorrectly force X to be immediately left of Y.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue uses "somewhere left of", "to the right of", "somewhere to the right of", etc.
zebralogic.example: Assuming X must be directly left of Y when the clue only said X is somewhere left of Y.

zebralogic.title: Adjacency without orientation (next to each other)
zebralogic.principle: Interpret "X and Y are next to each other" as |X − Y| = 1, with no implied left/right order. Without this, you may assign a fixed orientation that the clue does not specify.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue uses "next to", "adjacent", "are next to each other", etc.
zebralogic.example: Assuming X is left of Y when the clue only said they are next to each other.

zebralogic.title: Exact distance (houses between)
zebralogic.principle: For clues stating "There are N houses between X and Y", enforce |X − Y| = N + 1. Without this, you may treat the clue as a simple ordering and ignore the required gap.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue mentions a specific number of houses between two items.
zebralogic.example: Interpreting "There are 2 houses between X and Y" as merely X < Y, allowing them to be adjacent.

zebralogic.title: Combine consecutive adjacency constraints into a block
zebralogic.principle: When multiple clues create a chain of direct adjacencies (e.g., "A left of B" and "B left of C"), treat the involved items as a consecutive block of houses. Without this, you may leave gaps that violate the adjacency requirements.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When you have two or more adjacency clues that share a common element.
zebralogic.example: Placing A, B, C with a house between B and C despite clues stating B is directly left of C.

zebralogic.title: Equivalence linking
zebralogic.principle: When a clue states "X is the same as Y" (or "X is the person who ... Y"), treat it as a bidirectional equivalence linking the two attributes to the same house. Without this, you might assign X and Y to different houses.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue equates two descriptors (e.g., "the person who uses a Xiaomi Mi 11 is short").
zebralogic.example: Assigning the Xiaomi Mi 11 phone to one house and the short height to another house.

zebralogic.title: Fixed house assignment
zebralogic.principle: If a clue fixes an attribute to a specific house number (e.g., "the Samsung Galaxy S21 is in the second house"), enforce that exact placement. Without this, the attribute may be left free and violate the clue.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue mentions a house number explicitly.
zebralogic.example: Ignoring "Eric is in the first house" and placing Eric elsewhere.

zebralogic.title: Exclusion constraints
zebralogic.principle: Respect clues that forbid an attribute from a specific house (e.g., "Bob is not in house 4"). Without this, you might place the attribute in a prohibited location.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue uses "not in", "cannot be", "doesn't live in", etc.
zebralogic.example: Placing Bob in house 4 despite a clue stating he is not there.

zebralogic.title: Multi‑attribute equivalence
zebralogic.principle: When a clue links three or more attributes together (e.g., "the person who uses a Xiaomi Mi 11 is short and has child Alice"), treat all mentioned attributes as belonging to the same house. Without this, you might split them across different houses.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue mentions several attributes that all refer to the same person/house.
zebralogic.example: Assigning the Xiaomi Mi 11 phone to one house, the short height to another, and child Alice to a third house.

zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model often normalises text (e.g., title‑casing) instead of reproducing the exact token spelling from the problem.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Copy every attribute string verbatim from the clue text, preserving case, hyphens and spaces.

zebralogic.description: Capitalization mismatch for phone model values
zebralogic.why_it_happens: Brand names in phone models are frequently auto‑capitalised by the model, leading to mismatched tokens.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Treat phone model names as literal tokens and output them exactly as they appear in the puzzle.

zebralogic.why_it_happens: During single‑turn reasoning the model may overlook a clue or assume it is redundant, resulting in an assignment that violates the puzzle.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Systematically enumerate all clues, mark each as satisfied, and double‑check the final grid against every constraint before output.
